query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled post‐solidification low‐temperature annealing treatment that promotes the formation of a thin, ductile interfacial phase along the lamellar colony boundaries will reduce microcrack nucleation and thereby simultaneously improve room-temperature tensile strength and ductility in eutectic high-entropy alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloy with dual-phase lamellar colonies exhibiting numerous brittle interlamellar boundaries prone to microcrack initiation during room-temperature tensile deformation.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled low-temperature annealing treatment immediately after solidification, with parameters tuned to selectively modify the chemical and crystallographic nature of the lamellar interfaces without altering the bulk phases.
generation.conditions: The post-solidification annealing should be conducted at a low temperature (below bulk recrystallization thresholds) for an optimized duration, under inert or vacuum atmosphere, and testing should be performed at room-temperature tensile conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation or transformation of a thin, ductile interfacial phase at the lamellar colony boundaries.
generation.mechanism: By enhancing the cohesion and ductility at the interlamellar interfaces, the treatment reduces stress concentration sites and the propensity for crack initiation, thus preserving the high load-carrying capacity of the intrinsic lamellar phases while permitting greater plastic deformation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the unmodified alloy, the annealed sample is predicted to exhibit both a reduction in microcrack density and an improvement in room-temperature tensile ductility, with strength maintained or slightly enhanced relative to the untreated state.
generation.baseline: Conventionally processed eutectic high-entropy alloy with dual-phase lamellar colonies that shows high strength but limited ductility due to brittle interfacial boundaries.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effect is expected only when the annealing parameters are carefully controlled; excessive annealing may lead to coarsening of the bulk lamellae or formation of deleterious phases. The hypothesis is specific to eutectic high-entropy alloys with dual-phase lamellar microstructures and may not translate to alloys with different architectures.
generation.uncertainty: The exact annealing temperature, time window, and resultant phase characteristics at the interface that optimize both strength and ductility remain to be determined, requiring systematic parameter optimization.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of eutectic high-entropy alloy specimens: one group processed by conventional methods (baseline) and the other subjected to the proposed post-solidification low-temperature annealing treatment. Characterize the microstructure (using TEM/SEM) to verify the formation of a ductile interfacial phase, then perform standardized room-temperature tensile tests. Systematically vary annealing temperature and duration in a controlled study to delineate process windows.
measurements: Quantitative assessment of tensile strength and elongation to failure
Microcrack density and initiation sites via fractography
Interfacial phase thickness and structural coherence using TEM/SEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If samples receiving the annealing treatment do not show a statistically significant improvement in both room-temperature ductility and tensile strength (or if detrimental phases form at the interfaces leading to additional brittleness), the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Materials with high performance both at room and elevated temperatures are very attractive for a wide range of critical applications, potentially for aero-engine and fusion reactors [1] – [4] . For decades, ultra-strong, ductile, and heat-resistant materials have long been sought by the materials community, such as tungsten-based heavy alloys and nickel-based superalloys [3] , [5] . However, achieving alloys with an ultrahigh strength (>2 GPa) and a sufficient ductility (>10%) has presented a long-standing challenge. This has spurred significant research into metallurgical strategies to tailor microstructures for improved properties. One classical design paradigm is utilizing dilute concentrations of alloying elements, such as Re, Ti, and Cr, to improve the properties of W-based alloys; however, the “strength-ductility trade-off” has proven to be difficult to be solved with such single principal-element alloy systems due to the problem of brittle W-enriched phases with body-centered cubic (bcc) structures [5] , [6] . Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are a relatively new class of multicomponent materials that are based on several refractory metals, but may also contain other, generally low density, elements and typically have a body centered cubic (BCC) crystal structure [1] – [3] . These alloys have recently received much attention because of their attractive combination of properties not achievable by other classes of metallic alloys. For example, the first two RHEAs, NbMoTaW and NbMoTaVW, showed weak temperature dependence of yield strength in the temperature range from 600 °C to 1600 °C, with yield strength above 400 MPa at 1600 °C [4] , [5] . Unfortunately, these two alloys had high density (>12 g/cm 3 ) and further developments aimed at reducing the alloy density while keeping superior high-temperature properties. In the second generation RHEAs, high-density Ta and W were replaced with lower density refractory elements, such as Cr, Mo, Nb, V and Zr, and low density Al and Ti were added [6] – [13] . decision.trend: Early studies on eutectic high‐entropy alloys have largely focused on changing the bulk microstructure through conventional melting, casting, and thermomechanical processing (e.g., cold rolling, HIP, varying cooling rates) to boost strength. These treatments typically alter the relative phase distribution or refine the lamellar spacing, which improves strength but comes with a drastic loss in room‐temperature ductility. A later work (e.g., PMC5995863) attempted to re-engineer the microstructure (by inverting the phase roles) to recover ductility, but still used bulk processing methods that did not directly tackle the weak, brittle interlamellar boundaries. In short, while much effort has been directed at the overall architecture and phase fractions, the inherent weakness of the colony interfaces—where microcracks nucleate—remains insufficiently addressed.
decision.unsolved: The fundamental unresolved issue is that the dual‐phase lamellar colonies contain numerous internal boundaries which act as stress concentrators and crack‐initiation sites. All previous interventions, whether by modifying composition or bulk thermomechanical treatments, have improved either strength or ductility, but not both simultaneously, because they have not directly strengthened the interlamellar interfaces against microcrack formation.
decision.lever: Implement a controlled post‐solidification, low‐temperature annealing treatment specifically aimed at promoting the formation or transformation of a thin, ductile, interfacial phase along the lamellar colony boundaries. This lever would adjust the crystallographic structure and bonding at the interfaces without altering the bulk lamellar phases.
decision.why: This approach follows naturally from the trend: previous strategies modified overall microstructure or composition with trade‐offs in ductility and strength. By specifically engineering the interface—targeting the root cause of microcracking—the intervention is anticipated to blunt or arrest crack initiation, thereby improving both strength (by retaining the high load‐bearing capacity of the lamellae) and ductility (by allowing more plastic deformation before failure) relative to the unmodified lamellar state. Prior evidence about how interfacial characteristics influence deformation in complex alloys supports that enhancing boundary cohesion can reconcile the conflicting demands of strength and ductility.
